blocks.text: 1. Limitations of LLMs
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446706725-347791551.png
Why RAG Is Needed closed by pointing here. This topic widens that earlier, more specific discussion into the broader set of weaknesses RAG and other techniques address.
It surveys structural weaknesses that go well beyond the frozen knowledge problem alone.
2. Recapping The Preview
Limitations of LLMs was previewed in that earlier topic as the broader set of weaknesses RAG addresses.
This topic follows through on that promise, going through every detail only briefly gestured at before.
3. Recapping The Four Problems Already Covered
Frozen knowledge, private data, retraining cost, and transparency, all covered in Why RAG Is Needed, are themselves specific instances of broader LLM limitations.
This topic widens the lens to survey that broader structural picture.
4. Recapping Limited Context Window
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446706725-356270517.png
Even a huge context window, covered under Context Window's fixed maximum token count, still caps how much text a model can consider at once.
Entire large document collections cannot fit inside a single prompt at all, which is a real, structural limitation.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Limitation","Real consequence"],"rows":[["Limited context window","Large document collections cannot fit in one prompt"],["No external world access","Cannot browse, query, or check live data on its own"]]}

blocks.text: 5. No External World Access
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446706725-318558493.png
A plain language model cannot browse the web, query a database, or check live data on its own.
Every piece of information it uses has to already be inside its weights or its prompt.
6. Reasoning Limitations
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446706725-198617365.png
Multi-step, precise reasoning, especially over long chains of facts, remains error-prone.
Small mistakes early in a reasoning chain compound into larger errors later on, a separate limitation from the knowledge problems covered so far.
7. Cost Of Scale For Knowledge
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446706726-382559420.png
Storing more and more knowledge directly inside a model's weights requires larger models.
Larger models cost more to train and run, a practical scaling limitation covered in more depth under GPU Training.
8. Static Behavior Within A Single Conversation

blocks.alt: Static Behavior Within A Single Conversation
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446706726-54364249.png
Within a single generation call, covered under Inference, the model's weights cannot change at all.
Correcting a wrong belief mid-conversation requires new information to be fed back in explicitly.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This static behavior explains why RAG re-runs retrieval on every new query rather than relying on the model to remember or update anything on its own between turns.

blocks.text: 9. How RAG Addresses Several Of These Together

blocks.alt: How RAG Addresses Several Of These Together
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446706726-41484642.png
RAG, covered in What Is RAG, addresses limited knowledge, staleness, and lack of external access together.
Not every limitation disappears, but several real ones do.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Limitation","Does RAG address it"],"rows":[["Frozen, stale knowledge","Yes, through retrieval of fresh content"],["Multi-step reasoning errors","No, this requires separate reasoning techniques"]]}

blocks.text: 10. Recognizing Which Limitations RAG Addresses Versus Which It Does Not
RAG fixes knowledge gaps and external access limitations.
Reasoning limitations are a separate concern, requiring different techniques beyond RAG alone.
11. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates the limited context window problem, showing when a document collection exceeds what a prompt can hold.

code.content:
def estimate_tokens(text):
    # a simplified token count; see Tokenization for the real algorithm
    return len(text.split())

document_collection = [
    "Document one covers company policy on remote work arrangements.",
    "Document two covers the quarterly financial report summary.",
    "Document three covers the employee onboarding checklist.",
]

context_window_limit = 20  # a fixed maximum token count, see Context Window

def check_fits_in_context(documents, limit):
    total_tokens = sum(estimate_tokens(doc) for doc in documents)
    return total_tokens, total_tokens <= limit

total_tokens, fits = check_fits_in_context(document_collection, context_window_limit)
print(f"Total estimated tokens across all documents: {total_tokens}")
print(f"Context window limit: {context_window_limit}")
print(f"Fits entirely in one prompt: {fits}")
print("\nThis demonstrates why an entire document collection often cannot fit in a single prompt,")
print("motivating retrieval instead of stuffing everything in")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows a small document collection already exceeding a modest context window limit, motivating retrieval over trying to include everything at once.

blocks.text: 12. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a larger context window fully solves the problem of searching huge document collections.
Expecting a plain language model to check live data or query external systems on its own.
Treating RAG as a complete fix for multi-step reasoning errors, which require separate techniques.
Forgetting that a model's weights cannot change mid-conversation without new information fed back in.

blocks.text: 13. Key Takeaways

items: Limitations of LLMs surveys structural weaknesses broader than just the frozen knowledge problem.
Even a huge context window still caps how much text a model can consider at once.
A plain language model cannot browse, query, or check live data on its own.
Multi-step reasoning remains error-prone, with small early mistakes compounding into larger errors.
Storing more knowledge directly in weights requires larger, more costly models.
A model's weights cannot change within a single generation call, only across new input.
RAG addresses limited knowledge, staleness, and lack of external access, but not everything.
Reasoning limitations require separate techniques beyond RAG alone.
